article_title: Every Classroom, Every Day (ECED) — Reading
citation: Every Classroom, Every Day (ECED). (2019). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Designate an on-site instructional coach to monitor and support ECED implementation
description: ECED's staffing requirements state that implementation "Requires a designated on-site instructional coach or leader to monitor and support implementation", noting "This position may look different depending on size of school". Both curricula also "require a reallocation of existing school staff to teach each of the courses". The coach role is part of the program's implementation model rather than an evaluated manipulation in the outcome study.

Reallocation of existing school staff to teach the courses
constraints: The position may look different depending on size of school

examples: The evaluating study's ECED schools operated under this staffing model, with the coach supporting teachers across both program years.

article_title: Pirate Math
citation: Pirate Math. (2021). Evidence for Learning program summary. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org.au
title: Deliver supplemental math tutoring one-to-one outside ordinary math periods, staffed by teachers or trained paraprofessionals
description: Pirate Math delivers tutoring one-to-one, with tutors who may be teachers or paraprofessionals working with students outside of ordinary math periods. This staffing and scheduling model allows struggling third graders to receive intensive individual support without displacing their regular math instruction.
requirements: Paraprofessionals or certified teachers as tutors, with training provided through AIR
constraints: Requires scheduling sessions outside ordinary math periods, three per week over 16 weeks
target_learning_goals: Math calculations and word problem solving
examples: In the qualifying study, low-achieving students received 48 one-to-one sessions from teachers or paraprofessionals outside ordinary math periods.

article_title: JUMP Math
citation: JUMP Math — Evidence Rating: Promising. (2023). https://www.jumpmath.org
title: Use ongoing assessment to ensure comprehension before moving to new material
description: JUMP Math treats assessment as continuous: "Assessment is ongoing and considered essential to ensure comprehension before moving on to new material." This gates progression on demonstrated understanding rather than fixed pacing, complementing the program's stepwise mastery structure and individual pacing within a shared class concept.
requirements: Ongoing assessment embedded in the lesson sequence
target_learning_goals: comprehension of math concepts before progression
examples: Students do easier or more challenging work, or gain more practice, relating to the lesson concept until they are ready to move on.

article_title: Rethinking Teacher Evaluation
citation: Lauren Sartain, Sara Ray Stoelinga, and Emily Krone. (2010). Findings From the First Year of the Excellence in Teaching Project in Chicago Public Schools: Rethinking Teacher Evaluation. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/publications/Joyce_TE_yr1_finaldoc.pdf
title: Provide intensive, ongoing training and support for principals when implementing observation-based evaluation systems
description: The brief's implication section argues that realizing the Danielson Framework's potential as an evaluation tool requires ongoing training and support for principals. Even with roughly 50 hours of professional development in year one, principals still struggled to rate some components consistently. The authors warn that "If scale-up to a larger number of schools does not include training and support that is intensive and ongoing, there are likely to be problematic inconsistencies in the use of the Framework by principals."
requirements: High-quality, ongoing professional development for principals, including training sessions before and during the evaluation year
constraints: Principal turnover and the difficulty of providing extensive training when an initiative expands to all schools in a large district pose legitimate challenges
target_learning_goals: accurate and consistent evaluation of instructional practice
examples: In the pilot's first year, principals received three days of summer training, four half-day professional development sessions during the year, and monthly meetings to discuss the evaluation process

article_title: Transforming Teachers’ Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities
citation: Niess, M. L., & Roschelle, J. (2018). Transforming Teachers' Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities. Proceedings of the 40th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education, Greenville, SC. https://www.pmena.org/proceedings/
title: Online knowledge-building trajectory built on two tools and two processes
description: The online TPACK learning trajectory organizes professional learning around two tools and two processes within a social metacognitive constructivist framework. As printed, "Two tools support the online professional development: (1) a community of learners and (2) reflection," supporting social and cognitive presence; the two key processes are shared/individual knowledge development and inquiry learning, in which learners move between group and individual knowledge-building and investigate worthy questions. Reflection happens through reflective essays, peer reviews, and online portfolios.
requirements: Establishing a community of learners to support communication and interaction in the asynchronous online environment
Critical reflection activities such as reflective essays, peer review, and portfolios
constraints: The primarily asynchronous nature of online learning poses additional challenges for the design of these educational experiences
target_learners: in-service mathematics teachers in graduate online courses
target_learning_goals: reframing teacher knowledge for teaching mathematics with technologies
knowledge-building through inquiry and discourse
examples: In SED 520, teachers explored an unfamiliar temperature probe through ten laboratory experiments, discussed key questions in small communities of learners, and concluded each unit with a critical reflection

title: Teach one consistent routine for decoding multisyllabic words rather than a wide array of rules
description: The panel recommends choosing a single routine that gives students simple, reusable steps for tackling unfamiliar multisyllabic words. "Rather than teaching a wide array of rules, choose a routine that provides simple steps for breaking words into parts and blending those parts together to sound out the word." Teachers explicitly demonstrate the routine, guide students through applying it to several words, and post abbreviated steps or prompt cards so students can apply it independently across different words.

Post abbreviated steps of the routine or provide each student a prompt card

target_learning_goals: Accurately decoding complex multisyllabic words in grade-level texts
examples: Example 1.1 shows a teacher modeling a four-step routine of circling prefixes and suffixes, underlining vowel sounds, looping word parts while saying them, and blending the parts into a recognized word

article_title: Strengthening Principal Preparation Through On-The-Job Training: Insights from KIPP's Strategies for Developing Assistant Principals as School Leaders
citation: Jeff Archer, Jeffrey Max. (2019). Strengthening Principal Preparation Through On-The-Job Training: Insights from KIPP's Strategies for Developing Assistant Principals as School Leaders. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Develop principals through structured on-the-job training rather than relying on the assistant principal role alone
description: The publication's central design principle is that principal preparation can be strengthened through on-the-job training. As KIPP expanded, it met its need for school leaders by pairing a district-like talent pool of assistant principals with added strategies, so that "the assistant principal experience" becomes "a structured program for developing the skills required to serve as a school’s top administrator." Organizational strategies that structure their experience toward leadership skill development

examples: KIPP's expansion of its principal pipeline over two decades of rapid growth, using structured assistant principal development

article_title: Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education
citation: Jahneille Cunningham, Rebecca Colina Neri, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Building Mathematics Teachers' Capacity to Enact Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: School and district leaders should fund ongoing, high-quality professional development with collaborative inquiry to build teachers' CRSE capacity
description: The brief argues that professional development is the key lever for building teacher capacity for CRSE in mathematics, since teachers vary in experience and comfort with the approach. It specifies that PD should be ongoing, deepen mathematics content knowledge alongside CRSE understanding, and involve collaborative inquiry that situates teachers in a community of practice where they design lessons and experiment with new practices. Promising methods named include lesson study, funds of knowledge study groups, and empathy methods.
requirements: PD must be ongoing and involve collaborative inquiry, situating teachers within a community of practice with opportunities to design mathematics lessons and experiment with new instructional practices
constraints: These professional learning opportunities require sufficient resources and time
target_learning_goals: Enacting culturally responsive and sustaining education in mathematics instruction
examples: The brief names lesson study, funds of knowledge study groups, and empathy methods as promising PD approaches, and suggests organizing PD into tiers so teachers move from novice to intermediary to advanced levels of practice

article_title: Supporting California's Children through a Whole Child Approach: A Field Guide for Creating Integrated, School-Based Systems of Care
citation: Breaking Barriers, California Alliance of Child and Family Services, Santa Clara County Office of Education, & WestEd. (2022). Supporting California's children through a whole child approach: A field guide for creating integrated, school-based systems of care. https://WestEd.org/permissions
title: Use one-time funds for long-term-impact investments and plan early for sustainable funding
description: Because much of California's historic influx of funding is short term, the guide advises leaders to treat sustainability as a planning component from the start rather than a future goal. "Consider how to use these funds for short-term investments that can have long-term impacts, such as facilities or digital infrastructure, intensive short-term interventions for students, and staff capacity building." Leaders should also plan early for acquiring new resources or shifting existing long-term funding sources to sustain new initiatives, and Chapter 3 details blending and braiding funds across siloed streams.

constraints: If historic funding flows through the state's historically siloed system of separate agencies, LEAs and partners can expect the same barriers to integrated services
target_learners: Students and families served by LEAs using one-time federal and state relief funds
target_learning_goals: Sustained access to integrated academic, social-emotional, mental health, and health supports
examples: The guide notes professional development funding can bolster student-support staff positions and align school policies with PACEs science as disaggregated data reveal needs

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: Provide ongoing funding through school funding formulas because it is more predictable and sustainable than time-limited grants, especially for coordinative staffing
description: The report recommends ongoing investments through school funding formulas (set-asides or entitlement grants) because "ongoing funding is a more predictable and sustainable source of support for districts and schools than grant programs that might be discontinued—an especially important consideration for the additional coordinative staffing required to implement community schools." Multiyear and ongoing commitments matter because the community schools strategy is complex and takes time to fully implement. Grant funding can still be increased over time and can precede an ongoing stream.
requirements: A stable state funding mechanism (formula set-aside or entitlement grant) and funded coordinator positions at school and LEA levels.
constraints: Grant programs are time-limited and may be discontinued; the report presents grants as a precursor or complement, not a replacement, for ongoing funding.
target_learners: Students in high-need schools and districts receiving community schools funding
target_learning_goals: Sustained implementation of community schools programming and coordinative staffing
examples: Maryland's Concentration of Poverty entitlement grant provides annual personnel grants of $248,833 per eligible school; New York's Foundation Aid set-aside reached $250 million annually.

article_title: Increasing Access to Advanced Coursework in Texas
citation: Kristen Hengtgen, Hector Biaggi. (2024). Increasing Access to Advanced Coursework in Texas. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: OnRamps dual credit program (University of Texas)
description: OnRamps, established in 2011 by the University of Texas, offers virtual dual credit courses "taught by high school teachers but designed and supported by OnRamps staff and UT faculty." Courses require no placement assessment, so students whose test scores or grades may not convey readiness can still access advanced coursework, and students can choose to accept or decline college credit depending on their goals and performance. The program also offers free online professional development for virtual and hybrid educators on the TEA website and has served as a model for other institutions of higher education across Texas.
requirements: High school teachers deliver courses designed and supported by OnRamps staff and UT faculty
target_learners: Texas high school students, including those whose test scores or grades may not convey college readiness
target_learning_goals: Earning college credit and accessing college-level coursework while in high school
examples: OnRamps courses do not require a placement assessment, and students may decline college credit depending on their goals and course performance

citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: On the Rise Academy community-recruitment alternative certification program
description: On the Rise Academy, run by Detroit Public Schools Community District, "recruits new teacher candidates from the local community," with 75% of participants working in DPSCD as paraprofessionals, attendance agents, and academic interventionists. Candidates receive coaching cycles, observations, and intentional school placements under principals committed to their success. In 2021 about 90% of candidates were teachers of color, and DPSCD credits improvement in teacher vacancies partly to the Academy's pipeline of new teachers offsetting retirements and resignations.
requirements: Placements in buildings with principals who understand the model and support candidates
target_learners: Detroit community members and school support staff seeking certification
target_learning_goals: Teacher certification and effective classroom practice in Detroit schools
examples: DPSCD's chief human resources officer describes coaching cycles: candidates are observed and given feedback rather than "thrown into the wilderness."

article_title: A Comprehensive Review of the Changing Landscape of Academic Dishonesty in Automated Proctoring in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). A comprehensive review of the changing landscape of academic dishonesty in automated proctoring in the era of artificial intelligence. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01275-6
title: Key functionalities of online proctoring systems: eye gaze tracking, head pose estimation, facial recognition, user verification, activity recognition, and authentication
description: The review identifies a set of core functionalities that online proctoring systems implement, stating that "Some key functionalities involved in online proctoring are eye gaze tracking, head pose estimation, facial recognition, user verification, activity recognition, and authentication." These functionalities are typically implemented with camera-based monitoring and browser lockdown components; the review devotes separate sections to the algorithms and datasets used for each functionality and their reported accuracies and limitations.
requirements: Online proctoring commonly incorporates a camera-based monitoring component and a locking control (browser lockdown) that prevents examinees from opening new tabs.
constraints: The review notes that in large exam settings the efficiency of online proctoring systems is hindered by the inability of teachers to invigilate properly.
target_learning_goals: ensuring academic integrity in online examinations
detecting cheating behavior during remote assessments
examples: The review's Fig. 3 presents a classification of key functionalities of online proctoring systems, and Tables 3 and 4 analyze systems for eye gaze estimation and head pose estimation respectively.

article_title: Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving
citation: Sifatul Anindho, Videep Venkatesha, Jaclyn Ocumpaugh, and Nathaniel Blanchard. (2026). Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23317
title: Ordered network analysis (ONA) as a method for modeling directional temporal transitions among affective states in small, temporally coarse educational datasets
description: Ordered network analysis extends epistemic network analysis by incorporating temporal ordering into network construction, "allowing edges to represent ordered transitions between codes rather than unordered co-occurrence." The article applies ONA to retrospective cued-recall affect reports from a short situated CPS task, using a moving window of 2 events, groups as units of analysis, and difference networks to compare conditions. This makes ONA suited to modeling affect dynamics where the sequence of states is as informative as their co-presence, even in small datasets where descriptive summaries treat states as independent.
requirements: Timestamped self-report events so that ordered connections between codes appearing within a moving window can be constructed
constraints: Standard ENA collapses temporal order within windows; the article notes simultaneous co-occurring labels require an arbitrary fixed ordering, and small temporally coarse datasets limit what can be modeled
target_learners: adult learners collaborating in person on problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding dynamics of epistemic emotions during collaborative problem solving
examples: The study used the webENA tool with a moving window of 2 events; a sensitivity analysis with window sizes 2, 3, and 4 found consistent network structures
key_sources: Sifatul Anindho, Videep Venkatesha, Jaclyn Ocumpaugh, and Nathaniel Blanchard. (2026). Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23317

citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Move speech recognition on-device to make voice learning tools reach low-connectivity communities
description: The article's third lesson is that "Offline capability changes who the system can reach": moving ASR on-device was the decision that made the app relevant to low-connectivity settings, and accessibility and connectivity constraints are intertwined for this population. The core loop (transcription, lesson delivery, struggle detection, answer matching) operates without a network, with progress synchronizing opportunistically.
requirements: Locally cached lesson content and an embedded on-device ASR model
constraints: The design trades some on-device compute and storage for availability
target_learning_goals: uninterrupted access to spoken lesson delivery and feedback
examples: Kutti AI runs an embedded Whisper model on-device and caches lessons locally, syncing progress when connectivity returns

article_title: Towards sustainable AI knowledge-base assistants in computer science education: on-premise deployment and optimization with open educational resources
citation: Shen X, Feng L, Hua S, Liu D, Xie Z and Liu B (2026) Towards sustainable AI knowledge-base assistants in computer science education: on-premise deployment and optimization with open educational resources. Front. Psychol. 17:1843444. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1843444
title: On-premise OER-based AI knowledge-base assistant system for computer science education
description: A three-subsystem architecture comprising an LMS Layer, a Knowledge Base Layer with structured extraction and a FAISS vector index, and an AI Inference Layer with curriculum alignment and model optimization modules. The article states that "all components operate entirely on-premise on a consumer-grade GPU (RTX 3060, 12 GB VRAM), with no external API calls". It ingests 82 open-licensed Markdown documents (~347,000 tokens) from MIT OpenCourseWare, OpenStax, CS50 and WikiCS, and serves student queries via retrieval-augmented generation with quantized Qwen-7B or DeepSeek-MoE models.
requirements: Openly licensed OER documents (Creative Commons or OSI-compatible) as the knowledge corpus
A consumer-grade GPU with at least 12 GB VRAM for deployment
constraints: The article characterizes it as a knowledge-base assistant rather than a validated intelligent tutor; no controlled learner study was conducted
Evaluation dataset drawn from English-medium OER platforms; multilingual extension is future work
target_learning_goals: factual recall, concept explanation, and multi-hop reasoning about introductory computer science topics
examples: Deployed on an NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12 GB GDDR6) with Qwen-7B and DeepSeek-MoE variants, evaluated on 300 OER-derived queries

article_title: A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
citation: Yeager, D. S., Hanselman, P., Walton, G. M., Murray, J. S., Crosnoe, R., Muller, C., Tipton, E., Schneider, B., Hulleman, C. S., Hinojosa, C. P., Paunesku, D., Romero, C., Flint, K., Roberts, A., Trott, J., Iachan, R., Buontempo, J., Yang, S. M., Carvalho, C. M., Hahn, P. R., Gopalan, M., Mhatre, P., Ferguson, R., Duckworth, A. L. & Dweck, C. S. (2019). A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement. Nature 573. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1466-y
title: Short online growth mindset intervention module (two self-administered sessions)
description: A scalable, low-cost online module of two self-administered sessions of roughly 25 minutes each, delivered about 20 days apart during school hours, that teaches that intellectual abilities can be developed. It uses the metaphor that the brain is like a muscle, stories from older students and admired adults, and a self-persuasion exercise teaching the idea to a struggling future ninth-grader. The article states "The intervention consisted of two self-administered online sessions that lasted approximately 25 min each and occurred roughly 20 days apart during regular school hours". The module will be available at no cost to secondary schools in the United States or Canada via PERTS.

High implementation fidelity, achieved in the median school with 97% of screens viewed

title: Online homework platform enabling anonymized peer assessment distribution and in-class randomized experiments
description: A web-based homework platform developed by the authors through which students submitted homework responses and peer assessments. In treatment weeks, students "provided scores and comments on the homework responses of three peers" and received feedback from three peers; all responses and reviews were anonymized before distribution. Control students submitted online and were graded by instructors, with feedback delivered simultaneously to both groups and the same solution key provided.

article_title: Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion
citation: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x
title: On-line versus off-line methods for assessing strategy use
description: The article distinguishes two families of strategy-use assessment. On-line methods, such as thinking aloud, observation, eye-movement registration, and logfile registration, take "measurements taken concurrent to task performance" and code actual behavior against externally defined criteria. Off-line methods, such as questionnaires (e.g., MSLQ) and interviews, ask learners about strategy use before or after performance, so answers rest on reconstruction from memory of past experiences. The article uses this framework to evaluate the five special-issue instruments.
requirements: On-line methods need to be individually administered and coded according to a coding scheme; logfile coding systems must be validated with other on-line methods for each new task and learner group
constraints: Thinking aloud may be incomplete (tip-of-the-iceberg) and intrusive for poor readers; observations and logfiles capture only overt behavior; off-line methods risk memory failure and distortion
target_learners: learners during reading and text studying
target_learning_goals: assessment of cognitive and metacognitive strategy use
examples: Schellings' task-specific questionnaire and Bräten and Strømsø's MTSI are classified as retrospective off-line questionnaires; Magliano et al.'s RSAT indirect questioning is also off-line, with questions posed after each sentence disappears
key_sources: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x

article_title: A Meta-Analysis Investigating the Association Between Metacognition and Math Performance in Adolescence
citation: Gemma Muncer, Philip A. Higham, Corentin J. Gosling, Samuele Cortese, Henry Wood-Downie, & Julie A. Hadwin. (2021). A Meta-Analysis Investigating the Association Between Metacognition and Math Performance in Adolescence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09620-x
title: Online versus offline measurement as an organising distinction for metacognition assessment
description: The article organises metacognition measures by whether they capture metacognition during task performance or via retrospective self-report. "Offline measures are questionnaires that aim to capture an individual's self-reported perception of their own MC ability based on previous learning experiences", such as the MSLQ, MAI and Jr. MAI, whereas "online measures capture an individual's MC via ongoing behaviour and performance as they complete a task", including think-aloud protocols and behaviour observations. The article notes contested boundary cases (confidence judgements, calibration accuracy, JOLs) classified differently by Saraç and Karakelle, Veenman and van Cleef, and Craig et al., and reports poor correspondence between the two measure types in prior studies.
requirements: A measure must be classifiable as online or offline; the article applies the Veenman and van Cleef (2019) distinction, with think-aloud protocols and behaviour observations classed as online and self-report questionnaires as offline
constraints: The article states that online and offline measures may be measuring different facets of metacognition, given their poor correspondence across studies; classification of JOLs, confidence judgements and calibration scores is contested
target_learners: adolescents aged 11–16 in secondary school mathematics
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness, monitoring and regulation applied to mathematical problem-solving
examples: The review classified each included study's metacognition measure as online or offline (e.g. think-aloud protocols in van der Stel et al. as online; Jr. MAI questionnaires as offline) and used this categorisation in its moderation analysis

article_title: Evaluation of Evidence-Based Practices in Online Learning: A Meta-Analysis and Review of Online Learning Studies.
citation: Means, Toyama, Murphy, Bakia, & Jones. (2009). Evaluation of Evidence-Based Practices in Online Learning: A Meta-Analysis and Review of Online Learning Studies. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/reports.html
title: Conceptual framework for online learning along three dimensions: replacement vs. enhancement, learning-experience type, and synchronicity
description: The report develops a conceptual framework to guide its literature search and review, "identifying three key components describing online learning": (a) whether the activity serves as a replacement for or an enhancement to conventional face-to-face instruction, (b) the type of learning experience (expository, active, or interactive), and (c) whether communication is primarily synchronous or asynchronous. Exhibit 1 illustrates uses of online learning for each combination of these dimensions. The dimensions were derived from prior distance-learning meta-analyses.
requirements: Online learning applications must be classifiable on each of the three dimensions (objective, learning-experience type, synchronicity) for the framework to differentiate them.
constraints: The report notes the framework was derived from prior meta-analyses of distance learning and captures some of the most important kinds of variation, not all features; many other features such as setting, content type, and technology also apply.
target_learning_goals: Classifying and differentiating online learning applications when searching, reviewing, and evaluating online learning research and practice
examples: Exhibit 1 examples include a math course taught through online video lectures (expository, asynchronous, alternative) and professional development for science teachers through threaded discussions (interactive, asynchronous, enhancement).

citation: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059
title: Online figurative assessment tool measuring six inductive reasoning processes
description: A domain-general computer-based test of 54 figurative items, nine for each of Klauer's six inductive reasoning processes, administered through the eDia system. Item formats include class formation, odd-one-out, 4-fold cross classification, figural analogies, disturbed series, and matrices. The article reports that "The reliability of the whole test was high, Cronbach's alpha = .91" and that subtest reliabilities were acceptable.
requirements: Administration in school computer labs via the eDia platform within a 45-min lesson
constraints: Subtest reliabilities for Discrimination (.61) and Differentiating relationships (.63) were below .70

examples: The test was administered in schools' computer labs; average testing time was 26.6 min (SD = 7.0 min)

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Ontology framework of categories for analyzing, specifying, and coordinating student needs, theories, technologies, and best practices for theory-driven group formation
description: In the issue's final article, Isotani, Inaba, Ikeda, and Mizoguchi propose the reverse of designing an interaction space first: they "start from the individual students' educational needs and goals to then form group activities that are responsive to those needs." The paper presents "a framework or ontology of categories for analyzing, specifying, and coordinating student needs, theories, technologies, and best practices." The editorial stresses it is not trying to automate group formation but to support teachers as facilitators of collaboration and orchestrators of knowledge sharing.
requirements: Adequate support is required, since expecting teachers to match student needs to CSCL theories, technologies, and pedagogies without support is not feasible
constraints: Not intended to automate group formation; supports teachers in their facilitator role

target_learning_goals: Grouping students who can support one another and selecting personally tuned collaborative-learning activities
examples: Starting from individual needs, the authors hypothesize teachers can group students who support one another and select activities helping members achieve their goals as individuals and as a group

article_title: Does inquiry-based learning work better in regular classrooms or computer-based settings?
citation: Hasan Ozgur Kapici. (2025). Does inquiry-based learning work better in regular classrooms or computer-based settings? Instructional Science (2025) 53:705–728. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09711-0
title: Pair inquiry-based learning with technology-enabled scaffolding tools, since teacher guidance alone reaches students less individually
description: The article's discussion recommends that inquiry learning, especially for younger learners, be supported by online scaffolding tools such as hypothesis scratchpads and experiment design tools. It argues "teacher guidance may be less effective than online scaffolding tools, because teachers cannot follow each student in the classroom individually and cannot give appropriate feedback to them in the limited class time". Effective guidance in hypothesis formulation and experiment design is identified as a key factor in the experimental groups' success.
requirements: Scaffolding matched to inquiry phases (hypothesis generation, experiment design); teachers trained in IBL and virtual learning
constraints: The article also states a combination of inquiry-based methods and direct instruction is more effective than either alone, especially for younger learners

target_learning_goals: hypothesis formulation
experiment design
conceptual understanding
inquiry skills
examples: Experimental-group students used a hypothesis scratchpad with predefined domain terms and partial hypotheses, and an experiment design tool; control students developed hypotheses on their own with whole-class teacher guidance.

article_title: Go green: evaluating an XR application on biodiversity in German secondary school classrooms
citation: Mulders, M., Träg, K. H., & Kirner, L. (2025). Go green: evaluating an XR application on biodiversity in German secondary school classrooms. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09697-1
title: On Biodiversity's Tracks: greenpeace tablet-based VR application on the Amazon rainforest
description: On Biodiversity's Tracks (German: Der Artenvielfalt auf der Spur) is a virtual environment developed by greenpeace for classroom use, evaluated here in German secondary schools. It is "a virtual environment designed for classroom use that allows students to explore various places like the Amazon rainforest, the Great Barrier Reef, or a supermarket". Students scan a QR code, select South America on a globe, and freely explore a 360-degree rainforest environment with auditory and visual content and interactions with virtual agents, using touch gestures and body movements on their own tablets or smartphones.
requirements: Students need their own mobile device (tablet or smartphone) with touch input and headphones; exploration is only marginally accompanied by teachers, mainly for technical difficulties.

Interest in sustainability and the SDGs
Pro-environmental attitudes

article_title: The impact of an online tool for monitoring and regulating learning at university: overconfidence, learning strategy, and personality
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Kok, E. M., Lobbestael, J., & de Grip, A. (2017). The impact of an online tool for monitoring and regulating learning at university: overconfidence, learning strategy, and personality. Metacognition and Learning, 12, 21–43. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9159-5
title: Online Monitoring Exercise with feedback and 7-step Monitoring and Regulation Strategy (idea-unit self-testing technique)
description: A content-free, online intervention package for university students consisting of two separable components. The Monitoring Exercise has students read short texts with key concepts, type definitions, judge their quality, and then receive email feedback on over-, under- and correct estimations. The Monitoring and Regulation Strategy is a 7-step emailed guide that explains "how to assess their knowl- edge of key terms in textbooks by self-testing and comparing their definitions with the correct definition through counting idea-units" and emphasizes restudying unmastered concepts. In the study it was delivered via Surveymonkey and email across three faculties.
requirements: Delivered online via email and questionnaire tool; feedback email sent at most 3 days after the exercise
Strategy requires students to self-test, compare generated definitions with correct ones by counting idea units, and restudy unmastered key concepts
constraints: No guided practice with the strategy and no logging of strategy use was performed
Effects were examined in first-year undergraduate courses over 8 weeks

effective self-regulated study of textbook key concepts
examples: Students in the ME and ME-MRS conditions completed the exercise on texts titled 'Gestures' and 'Marriage', each containing four key concepts, and all but one participant overestimated their performance on at least one key concept (M = 4.95 overestimations).

article_title: Comparison of the work done in the successive minutes of a ten minute practice period in the fundamentals of arithmetic.
citation: Phillips, F. M. (1916). Comparison of the work done in the successive minutes of a ten minute practice period in the fundamentals of arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072031
title: A one-minute arithmetic test is a fair measure of pupil ability, but scores should be interpreted knowing first-minute output runs slightly higher
description: The article concludes that pupil ability in the fundamentals of arithmetic can be fairly determined by one minute of work, since first- and later-minute performance correlate highly. However, it cautions that "The product of the first minute is a little better than that of the later minutes, a point which should be borne in mind in giving a one minute test." Test designers should treat one-minute scores as valid but slightly elevated estimates.
requirements: Test administered as a timed one-minute period in the fundamentals, with pupils instructed to work as rapidly as possible
constraints: The first-minute advantage diminishes with repeated daily practice, so the elevation applies to initial rather than well-practiced testing
target_learners: Pupils in grades four through eight
target_learning_goals: Measuring computational ability in the four fundamentals of arithmetic
examples: The study administered two figure combinations in the four fundamentals, with 240 combinations per practice sheet, marking minute boundaries verbally during the ten-minute period

article_title: Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences
citation: Damien S. Fleur, Bert Bredeweg and Wouter van den Bos. (2021). Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences. npj Science of Learning 6:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00089-5
title: Online versus offline distinction in metacognitive processes
description: The article proposes distinguishing online metacognition — rapid, on-the-fly monitoring and control such as in EF tasks — from offline metacognition, which requires reflecting on past or future activities and developing meta-representations, as in metacognitive judgements. Within Nelson and Narens' framework, meta-knowledge is "the upward ﬂow from object-level to meta-level" and meta-control the downward flow. The authors state: "we propose to explicitly distinguish online and of ﬂine processes", noting the distinction is often not made explicitly but will help bridge cognitive neuroscience and educational sciences.
requirements: Requires clarifying which protocol assesses which construct, since it is unclear whether protocols operationalise online or offline processes
constraints: Offline metacognition is typically studied in school settings whereas EF evaluation is performed in the lab, limiting direct comparison
Educational sciences research typically does not frame metacognition in online/offline terms
target_learners: learners across educational settings studied in both disciplines, from primary schoolers to university students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and regulation of learning
examples: The review maps brain regions associated with meta-knowledge and meta-control onto online and offline categories, e.g. MFC and ACC for online meta-knowledge and aPFC and lPFC for offline processes

article_title: Statistical learning occurs during practice while high-order rule learning during rest period
citation: Romain Quentin, Lison Fanuel, Mariann Kiss, Marine Vernet, Teodóra Vékony, Karolina Janacsek, Leonardo G. Cohen and Dezso Nemeth. (2021). Statistical learning occurs during practice while high-order rule learning during rest period. npj Science of Learning 6:14. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00093-9
title: Distinct temporal dynamics account: statistical learning relies on online evidence accumulation while high-order rule learning requires rest-period consolidation
description: The article proposes that apparently simultaneous learning subcomponents have different short-scale temporal dynamics: statistical learning of probabilistic regularities is evidenced online during practice, while high-order rule learning of deterministic regularities is acquired offline during short rest periods. The authors state the results "suggest that the brain mechanisms leading to statistical and high-order rule learning are fundamentally different, the former requires online evidence accumulation while the latter requires a rest consolidation period." They offer two candidate explanations: high-order rule learning may need more attentional resources, or deterministic regularities may need rest to be consolidated, possibly rehearsed or replayed.
requirements: Distinguishing the learning types requires task designs with random, probabilistic, and deterministic transitions, such as the SRT and ASRT tasks used here
constraints: Future studies must dissociate whether the dynamic difference relates to the low-order/high-order or the probabilistic/deterministic nature of the learning, or a mixture of both
target_learners: healthy young adults in laboratory sequence-learning studies
target_learning_goals: implicit sequence learning
statistical learning of probabilistic regularities
high-order deterministic rule learning
examples: Three experiments using SRT and ASRT tasks with 506 behavioral sessions decomposed learning into online and offline gains via bin-level analysis

citation: Mavilidi, M.F., Paas, F., Zou, L., Lubans, D.R., Mokhtari, L., Schmidt, M., Castro Alonso, J.C., Ng, R., & Bennet, S. (2026). Effects of Videos with Whole-Body Movements on Young Children's Geography Learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00408-8
title: Online movement-based geography video intervention for young children (embodied cognition condition)
description: A digital learning session in which children watched a world-map video with animated cartoon animals and "engage in simple full-body movements, mimicking the animal movements shown in the video", such as jumping like a kangaroo or walking like an elephant while moving between continents, while verbally repeating continent names. requirements: Children verbally assenting plus written parental consent; quiet room at the museum; trained research assistants delivering pre-test, activity and post-test in order
constraints: Single learning session only; content limited to an introductory subset of geography competencies (naming continents and animals, locating them on a map)
conducted in small groups with a maximum of four children per session

examples: Both conditions watched each 5-min video twice for repeated exposure; the intervention group received additional opportunities to practise the animal movements

article_title: A Novel Framework for the Generation of Multiple Choice Question Stems Using Semantic and Machine-Learning Techniques
citation: Praveen Kumar, A., Nayak, A., Shenoy K., M., Chaitanya, & Ghosh, K. (2024). A Novel Framework for the Generation of Multiple Choice Question Stems Using Semantic and Machine-Learning Techniques. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00333-6
title: Mapping ontology rule consequent types onto Wh-type stem types (odd-one-out, T/F, synonym, definition, one-word)
description: Each DL or SWRL rule is first transformed into an Instance Tree (ITree); traversal then selects a stem template based on the consequent's variable type. The article specifies, for example, that "If the consequent is a 'Type variable', then the odd one out question stem generated is 'Which among the following is not a 'Type Variable'?'", while a 'theEquivalentNameOf' antecedent yields a synonym stem, a single property/class antecedent yields a definition stem, and multiple class variables yield a one-word stem. This pattern makes the ontology's rule structure directly determine which cognitive-level stem type is produced.

constraints: Stem variety is bounded by the consequent/antecedent configurations the article enumerates; question words map to specific Bloom cognitive skills per its Table 2
target_learners: students in technical domain courses (e.g., Operating Systems)
target_learning_goals: generating heterogeneous Wh-type MCQ stems assessing different cognitive levels
examples: For SWRL Example 1 the ITree traversal produced 'WHAT IS A/AN HARDWARE THAT HAS CONTROL OVER INPUT OUTPUT DEVICES?'; for DL Example 2 it produced the odd-one-out stem 'WHICH AMONG THE FOLLOWING IS NOT A/AN OPERATING SYSTEM?'

article_title: Keep Me in the Loop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data
citation: Di Mitri, D., Schneider, J., & Drachsler, H. (2022). KeepMeInTheLoop: Real-Time Feedback with Multimodal Data. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1093–1118. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00281-z
title: Limit real-time feedback to one message at a time with sufficient intervals to avoid overloading the learner
description: In real-time multimodal feedback systems, feedback should be fired one message at a time with sufficient lags between messages to prevent cognitive overload. The CPR Tutor assessed every chest compression but set its feedback frequency to 10 seconds, choosing audio as the least occupied sensory channel during CPR. This design was inspired by the Presentation Trainer, where the authors found it "more beneficial and less confusing for the user to fire one feedback message at a time".

constraints: The 10-second interval was chosen based on prior evidence and manual tuning, not optimised empirically in this study
target_learners: learners practising psychomotor skills with real-time feedback
target_learning_goals: correcting performance mistakes without cognitive overload
examples: The CPR Tutor fired audio feedback at most once every 10 seconds, sequencing five rule-based thresholds by mistake class

citation: Bruce M. McLaren, Sergey Sosnovsky, & Vincent Aleven. (2014). Preface - Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis - Part 1. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0021-0
title: Ontology- and semantic-web-based representation of domain knowledge in intelligent tutoring systems
description: The preface highlights semantic, ontology-based architectures as a characteristic research direction of Melis's. It notes that "ActiveMath was one of the first ITSs to heavily rely on ontologies and semantic web technologies for representing domain knowledge, modeling instructional content, and communicating between the components of the system." The same architectural idea appears in the special issue: the Lenat and Durlach tutoring system represents the teachable agent's erroneous or incomplete understanding as dedicated micro-theories within the CYC ontology, using the resulting conflicts to control agent behavior and guide learning.
requirements: Domain knowledge, instructional content, and inter-component communication must be represented via ontologies and semantic web technologies
target_learners: students using ontology-based intelligent tutoring systems for mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematics learning supported by semantically represented domain knowledge
examples: In the Lenat and Durlach system, the agent's erroneous or incomplete understanding is represented as dedicated micro-theories within the global CYC ontology

Preface - Emerging Technologies and Landmark Systems for Learning Mathematics and Science: Dedicated to the Memory of Erica Melis - Part 1. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0021-0

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking
citation: Friday Joseph Agbo, Solomon Sunday Oyelere, Jarkko Suhonen, Markku Tukiainen. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of a virtual reality game-based application to support computational thinking. Education Tech Research Dev 71:505–537. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10161-5
title: Participatory online co-design cycle embedded in design science research
description: The study embeds participatory design into the design science research methodology as the driver of the design, development, and demonstration phases. The article prints that "the online co-design process cycle involves planning, exploring, designing, discussing, and evaluating stages", which are iterative and strengthen research rigor within DSR. Online co-design was adopted because face-to-face meetings were not feasible during the Covid-19 pandemic, and it engages users and researchers to conceptualize, create, and prototype an artefact through an online environment.
requirements: Engagement of users and researchers in iterative online stages of planning, exploring, designing, discussing, and evaluating
constraints: Adopted to suit situations where face-to-face meetings between participants and researchers are not feasible
target_learners: higher education students co-designing educational games
target_learning_goals: computational thinking knowledge through co-designed mini games
examples: Mount Patti Treasure Hunt was conceptualized through a co-design process with students, building on a prior online co-design of mini games (Agbo et al., 2021a)

article_title: Interaction during online classes fosters engagement with learning and self-directed study both in the first and second years of the COVID-19 pandemic
citation: Gherghel, C., Yasuda, S., & Kita, Y. (2023). Interaction during online classes fosters engagement with learning and self-directed study both in the first and second years of the COVID-19 pandemic. Computers & Education, 200, 104795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104795
title: Design online classes with deliberate opportunities for social interaction, because interactivity fosters engagement and spillovers into self-directed study
description: The article's core design recommendation is that online lecturers should structure classes to include social interaction opportunities such as group work, discussions, and presentations. The study found that "participants who reported that the classes they had attended had more group work, discussions, and presentations (social interaction), also reported that they enjoyed the classes more" and put in more effort, with indirect effects on out-of-class self-directed study. Because what happens during online classes can affect learning outside class, lecturers should be aware that class structure influences students' broader learning behavior.
requirements: Online course delivery must include activities that create opportunities for interaction among students and between students and instructors, such as group work, discussions, and presentations.
constraints: The article cautions that "the more the better" is not always the case, that interaction quality matters, and that introverted or socially anxious students may find interactive courses burdensome.
target_learners: First-year university students in online courses
target_learning_goals: Learning engagement with online classes
Self-directed learning skills
examples: The study measured perceived opportunities for social interaction during online classes with five items including pair work and group work, and found interactivity predicted engagement and self-directed study time in both 2020 and 2021.
key_sources: Gherghel, C., Yasuda, S., & Kita, Y. (2023). Interaction during online classes fosters engagement with learning and self-directed study both in the first and second years of the COVID-19 pandemic. Computers & Education, 200, 104795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104795

article_title: Explicit video-based instruction enhanced students’ online credibility evaluation skills: Did storifying instruction matter?
citation: Kiili, C., Kiili, K., Räikkönen, E., & Coiro, J. (2025). Explicit Video-Based Instruction Enhanced Students' Online Credibility Evaluation Skills: Did Storifying Instruction Matter?. Computers and Education, 229, Article 105252. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105252
title: Bidirectional model and CORE framework of online credibility evaluation strategies
description: The article organizes online credibility evaluation through two frameworks: the bidirectional model of first- and second-hand evaluation strategies, which "distinguishes content and source evaluation strategies", and the CORE framework, which "extends the bi-directional model by adding the strategy focusing on evaluation of context". Together they frame credibility evaluation as reciprocal and iterative use of content strategies (knowledge-based, discourse-based, corroboration), source strategies (expertise, benevolence), and context strategies. The study's instruction targeted content and source strategies—author's expertise, author's intentions, and quality of evidence—and its outcome task incorporated knowledge-based and contextual evaluation.
requirements: Instruction and assessment must operationalize the distinct evaluation strategies (content, source, context) so learners can practice them one at a time
constraints: The bidirectional model was developed for readers evaluating conflicting multiple scientific texts; the CORE framework situates evaluation within the internet environment
target_learning_goals: online credibility evaluation skills
justifying credibility evaluations
examples: The study's videos taught author's expertise, author's intentions, and quality of evidence strategies, and the evaluation task measured confirming, questioning, and justifying credibility

article_title: Media multitasking, online vigilance and academic performance among students in three Southern African countries
citation: le Roux, D.B., Parry, D.A., Totolo, A., Iyawa, G., Holloway, J., Prenter, A., Botha, L. (2021). Media Multitasking, Online Vigilance and Academic Performance among Students in three Southern African Countries. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104056
title: Online vigilance as a construct of psychological connectedness to online content
description: Online vigilance, as proposed by Reinecke et al. (2018) and adopted by this article, "describes individual diﬀerences in users’ cognitive orientation to online connectedness, their attention to and integration of online-related cues and stimuli, and their prioritisation of online communication". It is measured with the Online Vigilance Scale, comprising salience, monitoring and reactivity subscales. Its key property is distinguishing technological from psychological connectedness: some users develop higher vigilance despite comparable media use. The article tests it as a predictor of academic performance alongside media use behaviours.
requirements: Assessed with the 12-item Online Vigilance Scale (salience, monitoring, reactivity subscales), responses averaged across items
constraints: The article distinguishes online vigilance from Internet or technology addiction, describing it as involvement that does not necessarily impair functioning or mental health
No prior studies had investigated its relationship with academic performance before this study
target_learners: University undergraduate students in South Africa, Botswana and Namibia
target_learning_goals: Understanding how students' psychological orientation to online connectedness relates to academic performance
examples: The survey administered the Online Vigilance Scale to 1445 undergraduates and regressed academic performance on it together with media use variables

article_title: What seams do we remove in mobile-assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature
citation: Lung-Hsiang Wong, Chee Kit Looi. (2011). What seams do we remove in mobile assisted seamless learning? A critical review of the literature. Computers and Education. https://hal.science/hal-00696239
title: One-or-more-mobile-device-per-learner setting supporting seamless learning
description: The article situates its work relative to a proposed seamless learning model supported by equipping each learner with one or more mobile device. It states it is "Inspired by the exposition by Chan, Roschelle, Hsi, Kinshuk, Sharples, Brown, et al. (2006) on the seamless learning model supported by the setting of one or more mobile device per learner." This per-learner device setting is the technological basis the review takes as the context for mobile-assisted seamless learning practice.
requirements: One or more mobile devices per learner to support the seamless learning model
constraints: The article presents this setting as an inspiration from prior work (Chan et al., 2006), not as its own empirical finding
target_learners: learners equipped with one or more mobile devices each
target_learning_goals: supporting seamless integration of learning experiences across contexts
examples: The review investigates how to put seamless learning into practice under this per-learner mobile device setting

article_title: Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies
citation: Ardid Ramírez, M.; Gómez-Tejedor, JA.; Meseguer Dueñas, JM.; Riera Guasp, J.; Vidaurre, A. (2015). Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies. Computers and Education. 81:296-303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.10.010
title: In blended assessment, treat the administration mode of online exams as a design decision that changes scores
description: The study uses online exams "in three different situations: in an evaluation-proctored exam, in an evaluation-unproctored exam and as a training-homework task" within blended assessment. Because marks clearly differ by mode, and unproctored results are biased toward higher ratings with greater dispersion, instructors designing blended assessment should select and interpret online exam administration modes deliberately rather than treating online scores as mode-independent.
requirements: The same online exam instrument must be applied under explicitly chosen administration conditions (proctored, unproctored, or as homework).
constraints: The article's comparison covers the three studied situations; unproctored results carry a stated bias towards higher ratings and greater dispersion.
target_learners: university students in physics-related engineering coursework
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of student performance in blended courses
examples: The article studied online exams as a proctored evaluation exam, an unproctored evaluation exam, and a training-homework task, finding marks depend on the mode.

article_title: Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies
citation: Ardid Ramírez, M.; Gómez-Tejedor, JA.; Meseguer Dueñas, JM.; Riera Guasp, J.; Vidaurre, A. (2015). Online exams for blended assessment. Study of different application methodologies. Computers and Education. 81:296-303. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.10.010
title: Online exams as a component of blended assessment
description: Online exams are used "as part of the evaluation process in the context of blended assessment," complementing conventional evaluation. The article studies their deployment in three situations: evaluation-proctored, evaluation-unproctored, and training-homework use. The element's outcomes depend on administration mode, making mode specification a necessary part of its design.
requirements: A specified administration mode (proctored, unproctored, or homework) must accompany any use of the online exam for evaluation.
constraints: Unproctored application introduces a bias towards higher ratings and greater dispersion of results compared with proctored application.
target_learning_goals: course evaluation and training through online assessment
examples: Online exams were deployed in the studied course in an evaluation-proctored exam, an evaluation-unproctored exam, and as a training-homework task.

article_title: The relationship between class size and online activity patterns in asynchronous computer conferencing environments
citation: Hewitt, J., & Brett, C. (2007). The relationship between class size and online activity patterns in asynchronous computer conferencing environments. Computers & Education, 49, 1258-1271. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2006.12.003
title: Recommended online class size limits of roughly 8 to 30 students rest on practitioner experience, not empirical evidence
description: The article's background review reports that online-learning researchers have proposed upper and lower limits on class size: Hiltz, Rovai, and Aragon propose thirty as an upper limit, Turoff proposes a need for critical mass, and Rovai suggests 8-10 students are required minimally for good interactions. The article states "the ideal class size appears to be somewhere between 8 and 30 students, depending on the type of course", representing a tradeoff between lively discussion and feeling overwhelmed. However, it emphasizes these recommendations are based on the researchers' own teaching experiences rather than formal research.
requirements: Enough members to support lively discussion without so many participants that people feel overwhelmed
constraints: The article states these claims and recommendations appear to be based on researchers' own online teaching experiences, with little formal research conducted in this area
target_learners: adult online learners in distance education courses
target_learning_goals: sustained online discussion and peer interaction
examples: The article cites Hiltz's (1997) recommendation to divide conferences into subgroups when student numbers reach or exceed thirty

article_title: Identity profile of young people experiencing a sense of risk on the internet: A data mining application of decision tree with CHAID algorithm
citation: Muñoz-Rodríguez, J. M., Patino Alonso, C., Pessoa, T., & Martín-Lucas, J. (2023). Identity profile of young people experiencing a sense of risk on the internet: A data mining application of decision tree with CHAID algorithm. Computers & Education, 197, 104743. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104743
title: Onlife experience as the theoretical frame for young people's internet-related identity and risk
description: The article adopts Floridi's (2015) notion of onlife experience, living, and identity, arguing that a large part of a young person's life takes place online and that the boundary between online and offline worlds is becoming blurred. Within this frame, the internet is not a mere tool but the spatiotemporal setting where young people occupy and act, relate, move and communicate, making identity-building processes vulnerable to risks young people often do not perceive. The study's findings are read as corroborating that the cohort lives onlife and lacks critical thinking and sense when acting online.
requirements: Research on young people's internet use should treat online experience as an everyday setting for coexisting, acting and relating rather than contrasting online and offline lives.
constraints: The article notes its conclusions are subject to an obvious risk of obsolescence in the medium run due to rapid technological change.
target_learning_goals: Developing critical awareness of risks associated with internet use
Building a healthy and responsible relationship with technologies

citation: Alegre, E., Penman, A., Unicomb, R., & Scarinci, N. (2025). International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders, 60(3), e70040. https://doi.org/10.1111/1460-6984.70040
title: Provide ongoing education, supportive work environments and opportunities for familiarity with people who stutter to enhance SLP competence in stuttering management
description: The review's clinical implications emphasise "the importance of ongoing education and support for SLPs to enhance their clinical competence in stuttering management". Specifically, targeted professional development, supportive work environments and familiarity with people who stutter can positively impact SLPs' confidence and proficiency. The review recommends SLPs whose caseloads include stuttering prioritise ongoing education, seek support to implement treatment where needed and pursue opportunities to gain experience with people who stutter.
requirements: SLPs whose caseloads include stuttering need access to targeted professional development and supportive work environments
constraints: The review notes it is unclear whether continuing professional education improves actual competence or only perceived competence
target_learning_goals: clinical competence in stuttering assessment and treatment

article_title: Effectiveness of education and training programmes to help clinicians assess and classify perineal tears: a systematic review.
citation: Simpson G, Philip M, Richards A, Eggleston AJ, Vogel JP, Wilson AN, Homer C. (2025). Effectiveness of education and training programmes to help clinicians assess and classify perineal tears: a systematic review. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-095961
title: Embed ongoing review of practice into training programmes to maintain knowledge and skills.
description: The review concludes that ongoing review of practice appears to be crucial for maintaining knowledge and skills. The Norwegian quality improvement intervention, which included supervised hands-on learning and ongoing review of practice, reported dramatic reductions in severe perineal tears. Future programmes should take into consideration the framework and lessons learnt from the original Norwegian programme.
requirements: Programmes should incorporate ongoing review of practice following initial training.
constraints: The duration of effective training to impact perineal tear rates was not clear from the data available.
target_learning_goals: Maintenance of perineal tear assessment and classification skills

citation: Karalar, H., & Korucu, A. T. (2016). Effects of Semantic Web Based Learning on Pre-service Teachers' ICT Learning Achievement and Satisfaction. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(8). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i8.1676
title: Ontology-driven prerequisite objective analysis for meaningful learning in SWBL
description: The article grounds SWBL in cognitive theories of meaningful learning: prerequisite knowledge activated as a foundation for new knowledge, and learning promoted when new information relates to existing schemas. OntoExcel encodes classes, object properties (hasLO, hasPrerequest, isLoOf, hasObjectiveOf, isObjectiveOf) and inverse properties so the pedagogical agent can determine which objectives are prerequisites or become difficult unless prior objectives are learned. Objective analysis was conducted for each objective before learning objects were assigned.
requirements: a domain ontology defining classes, properties and relations between objectives
objective analysis determining prerequisites before learning objects are presented
constraints: the article states there is not enough learning environment at the expected level due to lack of development in standard ontologies and incapability of different systems working at the same time
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of structured ICT objectives with explicit prerequisite relations
examples: The ontology was developed through Noy & McGuinness's stages, asking questions such as what are the objectives of a chosen topic and what are the prerequisite objectives of this objective

article_title: Econometric Assessment of "One Minute" Paper as a Pedagogic Tool
citation: Amaresh Das. (2010). Econometric Assessment of 'One Minute' Paper as a Pedagogic Tool. International Education Studies, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v3n1p17
title: One-minute paper classroom feedback technique
description: A low-tech classroom assessment technique in which, in the final minute or two of class, students answer two questions: what was the most important thing learned and what is the muddiest point remaining. The instructor reads and analyzes responses (here in an Excel spreadsheet) and opens the next class by reviewing frequently mentioned muddy points. The article describes it as "a modest, relatively simple and a low-tech innovation that can improve student's learning and active participation in class".
requirements: Administered at the conclusion of each class period with responses collected anonymously in a box or by e-mail
Instructor analyzes responses and reviews muddy points at the beginning of the subsequent class
target_learning_goals: improving student learning of course content
active participation in class
examples: In Spring 2006 the technique was used in only one of two statistics sections; in Fall 2005 it was used in both sections.

citation: Wouter Smets. (2017). High Quality Differentiated Instruction – A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2074-2080. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051124
title: Use ongoing formative assessment both as assessment of learning and as assessment for learning in differentiated instruction
description: The checklist requires that the teacher gathers assessment data on what has been learned and uses this in future teaching design. During the learning process the teacher provides ongoing formative assessment giving students insight into what has and has not been learned, and creating the opportunity to adapt lessons. The article states the assessment data are "not only an assessment of learning but also an assessment for learning".
requirements: Teachers must gather assessment data on what has been learned and use this in future teaching design
target_learners: general education teachers and their students

examples: In the article's third illustration, a teacher team realizes it lacks assessment data for prior-knowledge-tailored assignments and decides to install formative assessments

citation: Williams, R. D., Jr., Barnes, J. T., Holman, T., & Hunt, B. P. (2013). Substance Use Prevention Among At-Risk Rural Youth: Piloting the Social Ecological One Life Program. The Journal of At-Risk Issues, 18(1).
title: One Life: a school-based social ecological group mentoring program
description: One Life is a school-based group mentoring program for at-risk rural youth built on the social ecological model, targeting intrapersonal influences on drug use. It comprised "a lighted schoolhouse, life-coaching, and career planning" implemented over four months, with mentors drawn from trained local university students. Groups of four to six participants met biweekly in 45-60 minute sessions combining a developmental assets curriculum with tutoring.
requirements: Trained mentors with college-credit coursework in mentorship and school-district background checks
Collaboration with regional institutions including school districts, the youth judiciary system, and a regional support center
constraints: Self-selection of subjects and a relatively homogenous population limited generalizability
target_learning_goals: reduce substance use
increase interest in higher education
develop social skills

article_title: Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited
citation: Zambak, V. S., Alston, D. M., Marshall, J. C., & Tyminski, A. M. (2017). Convincing Science Teachers for Inquiry-Based Instruction: Guskey's Staff Development Model Revisited. Science Educator, 25(2), 108-116. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143566
title: One-year IBI-focused professional development program
description: Seventy middle school science teachers from a southeastern state were recruited to be part of a PD program designed to improve the quality of IBI. Teachers were provided two weeks of teacher training in the summer, four whole group follow-up sessions during the academic year, four or more full-class observations with debriefing after, and numerous individual support sessions. The emphasis for the summer portion of the PD program and the follow-up meetings was to provide the teachers with modeled IBI lessons, ensure opportunities to reflect on IBI lessons, and collaborate to design inquiry-based lessons that could be implemented.
requirements: The program required two weeks of teacher training in the summer, four whole group follow-up sessions during the academic year, four or more full-class observations with debriefing after, and numerous individual support sessions.
constraints: Forty science teachers who were teaching in 10 different middle schools became the participants for this study; only the first year data were used.
target_learning_goals: implementing inquiry-based instruction
examples: The planning model that the program encouraged teachers to use was the 4Ex2 Instructional Model (Marshall, Horton, & Smart, 2009), an adaptation of the 5E Instructional Model.

citation: Chappell, S., Arnold, P., Nunnery, J., & Grant, M. (2015). An Examination of an Online Tutoring Program's Impact on Low-Achieving Middle School Students' Mathematics Achievement. Online Learning, 19(5). https://jolt.merlot.org/2015/vol11no2.htm
title: Embed systematic progress monitoring and individualized learning plans in online tutoring programs serving struggling mathematics students
description: The article's tutoring program used diagnostic assessments before tutoring to develop individualized learning objectives and a flexible learning plan for each student, aligned with school curricular standards. The article states the program "focuses on individualized progress monitoring to design and adjust tailored interventions," and the authors recommend that online tutoring programs incorporate specific postsession prompts to ensure systematic attention to student data.
requirements: Tutors must administer diagnostic assessments before tutoring begins to develop individualized learning objectives
Learning plans must be aligned with the school's curricular standards and scope and sequence
In-session assessments must allow tutors to assess student progress by specific skill in a formative manner
constraints: The study context involved schools already implementing a school-wide mathematics program addressing Tier 1 and Tier 2 RTI supports, so effectiveness as a standalone intervention is not established

schema development in mathematics problem solving
examples: The Focus EduVation program administered diagnostic assessments before tutoring, created individualized learning plans aligned with school curricular standards, and used in-session formative assessments and posttests to examine overall growth.

citation: Skipper, Y. (2015). An evaluation of an intervention to change first-year psychology students' theory of intelligence. Psychology Teaching Review, 21(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1080279
title: One-hour brain plasticity presentation intervention with memory-based control
description: The intervention consisted of two parallel one-hour PowerPoint presentations, each containing information and an activity. The intervention presentation presented research showing "effort and technique were vital to success", including Ericsson's violinist study and Maguire's taxi driver MRI study on brain plasticity. The control presentation covered memory research, including music and drugs effects, to keep the experience as similar as possible between groups.
requirements: Both presentations must be one hour long and contain information and an activity
Delivery by the same teacher to all groups
constraints: The deception-based pen pal design used by Aronson et al. (2002) was not reusable across year groups, motivating this simpler presentation format
target_learning_goals: incremental theory of intelligence
learning goals
task choice intentions
examples: Students completed a Mantyla (1986) word-list cue activity, explained as brain plasticity in the intervention group and as a memory technique in the control group

article_title: Automated Formative Evaluations for Reading Comprehension in an English as a Foreign Language Course: Benefits on Performance, User Satisfaction, and Monitoring of Higher Education Students in Chile

title: One-day VT/CME course combining theoretical input, self-reflection, and improvisation-based communication training
description: A reusable course format for training practising GPs and GP trainees in existential communication with cancer patients. The intervention was "designed as a one-day VT/CME course (eight hours)" and comprised three basic elements: theoretical input on existential frames and patient needs, reflection in groups and self-reflective exercises such as "What is the existential to me?", and communication training using theatre improvisation with professional actors and facilitated feedback. Evaluation showed significant self-efficacy gains and positive participant evaluations.
requirements: Taught by experienced teachers in existential philosophy, psychology and religious/spiritual coping
Professional actors and a facilitator to run the improvisation scenes and moderate audience feedback
A question/supportive communication tool incorporated into the curriculum
constraints: Tested only on a small scale (twenty participants, one Danish region) prior to a planned large-scale RCT
Voluntary participation risks selection bias toward GPs open to communication training
target_learners: Residents in training to become GPs
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of existential, religious and spiritual patient needs
Self-awareness of own existential values and barriers
Confidence and skill in existential communication
examples: The course was piloted with twenty GPs at a regional conference venue, with questionnaires before and just after and telephone interviews within four weeks
